inline.s: The potential of human life is, in truth, something we have scarcely noticed or developed in ourselves. If these potentials could be developed, it would be a leap forward for humankind itself! Self-hypnosis meditation therapy is one basic method for developing this potential. I have read a number of related works. Among them, the method taught by the famous Western hypnotherapist Dr. Weiss goes like this:
Lie on a bed or in a reclining chair. Imagine that you are sleeping in a place you consider very beautiful and very comfortable. Then command yourself to fully relax your whole body, step by step:
Relax your head...
Relax your neck...
Relax your body...
Relax your hands...
Relax your hips...
Relax your feet...

Then imagine a beam of white light full of energy shining throughout your whole body (those who are ill may focus the light on the affected part). Under the light's illumination, every place the light touches is washed clean; germs are all destroyed; every cell is filled with vitality...
In this way, in a state of complete relaxation, meditate for
minutes or more (even without the perseverance for

minutes, a spell of meditation is still good). You can do this meditation before sleep, until you fall asleep. You can also meditate for a while after waking before getting up. Better still, you can recharge with meditation at any time during the day. (This is not the only method. For example, you can imagine water cleansing your whole body instead of light.)
This method suits ordinary people for maintaining health, and also suits the sick for treating themselves. Persevere, and the effects will be plain to see!
In another book I read, there were clinical cases of meditation therapy by several famous Chinese physicians. One of them goes like this:

The physician instructed the patient to meditate every day (meditation should always be done in a state of full bodily relaxation as described above): imagine that within your body there is a silver needle ceaselessly piercing the tumor inside you. It pierces the tumor full of holes, and the tumor slowly dissolves... Then it naturally grows smaller and smaller... smaller and smaller... Three months later, the patient went for an
X
-ray examination, and amazingly discovered that the tumor was gone! The patient had actually resolved that tumor by himself through meditation therapy!

Before long, some days later, the patient came again, saying that it still hurt inside his body. So the physician examined him once more, yet could find nothing wrong. Later the physician thought and thought, and finally it came to him in a flash! He told the patient: imagine again, and dissolve that silver needle, then expel it along with your waste. After that, the patient indeed felt no more pain. The great inventor Edison was also skilled at meditation. He liked to sit in a high-backed chair to meditate. While meditating, his right hand would hold a metal ball, and on the floor below was placed a metal basin. This was to keep him from falling asleep during meditation. For once he fell asleep, the metal ball in his right hand would drop into the basin and wake him, and then he would go on meditating. Edison, however, did not use meditation to preserve health or cure illness, but to gain inspiration for his inventions. It seems he too was another outstanding success who developed his potential through meditation!
The Buddha said, "All dharmas are mind!"

So-called imagination therapy means that patients themselves build up the confidence and courage to struggle against illness, establishing in their minds a firm belief in certain victory - and this belief must remain constant and unchanging.

Through imagination, patients can increase the number of immune cells in the body, so that the body's immune function improves and the progress of disease is effectively restrained. The principle may be that imagination establishes a fixed channel of connection between the brain and the body's immune system, forming a focus of excitation beneficial to the body, thereby easing invisible mental pressure and promoting physical and mental recovery.

At present, imagination therapy has abroad become a necessary prescription for treating cancer, and it has achieved good results. For example, in the United States there was a woman patient with a malignant tumor on her neck; the doctors concluded that she had only

months to live. Later, on the advice of a psychiatrist, the patient adopted "imagination therapy." Every day she sat quietly on her bed, free of distracting thoughts, concentrating on imagining that the tumor on her neck was a demon, while the white blood cells in her body were very valiant knights brandishing sharp swords to attack the demon, wiping the demons out one by one. Every day she imagined this
times. A year later, the patient not only did not die, but miraculously recovered. According to reports,
cancer patients whom doctors had declared to have less than a year to live, after treatment with imagination therapy, mostly lived at least
months, and
of the patients partly or fully recovered their health.

blocks.text: Imagination Therapy Can Strengthen the Body's Immunity

inline.s: Someone once conducted an experiment like this: when a person imagines riding a bicycle, the blood flow in the lower limbs increases relatively. This shows that imagination can produce physiological effects.

A person's emotions and psychological state strongly influence the functioning of the immune system, and the immune system interacts through hormones and certain other factors in the blood; the positive emotions and good frame of mind brought by imagination therapy strengthen resistance to illness precisely through the immune system. In recent years the medical world has clinically promoted a new therapy that uses imagination as its technique, letting patients, through imagination, bring the organism at last to an active process of defending against and overcoming disease. It differs from empty fantasy and aimless random thinking; rather, it applies imagination in a targeted and selective way in order to strengthen the body's immune capacity.

There was a man who had undergone two cancer operations and had been given a "death sentence" by his doctors. He often imagined that the white blood cells in his body were invincible valiant warriors, trading blow for blow with the seemingly powerful cancer cells, beating and destroying them all; and so he has lived healthily for
years.

Imagination rich in feeling and love has a beneficial effect on heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure. Relaxed imagination can help relieve illnesses caused by mental tension, and imagination therapy can even conquer cancer. A frail, sickly middle-aged man, under a doctor's guidance, three times a day imagined his body growing stronger day by day, and as a result his condition eased markedly - which shows the marvelous effect of imagination therapy.

Researchers hold that the human body is a particularly complex organism concealing an enormous potential for health, and that a person's energy and abilities are generally only developed and used to the extent of

%; one can write, paint, and work with one's mouth or feet. Imagination therapy can produce certain positive physiological changes in the body; through imagination one can markedly strengthen resistance to illness and raise immune function. This is the important material basis on which imagination therapy cures disease.

Imagination therapy draws on the full dynamic power of consciousness, spirit, and psyche over the body's own physiological functions. For example, when someone falls ill with a certain disease, though his constitution may still be sound, if his spirit collapses first, then even a miracle cure is of no avail. Yet some people, though afflicted with a terminal illness, can face it with an open heart and a strong will, struggling against the demon of disease, and in the end come back from the brink of death. The nerve center of imagination lies in the right hemisphere of the brain; when a person engages in imaginative activity, it can weaken the right hemisphere's inhibitory effect on the immune system, thereby strengthening the body's immune function and helping it fight disease.

The belief produced by imagination can bring a person tremendous power. For example, when an insomniac takes a sleeping pill (actually a placebo), the false passes for true, and yet the patient can quickly fall into a peaceful sleep. There are many similar examples, and data indicate that combining imagination therapy with standard treatment is superior to applying standard therapy alone.
, a daughter was born into a wealthy Swedish family. Yet before long the child contracted an inexplicable form of paralysis and lost the ability to walk.

One day the girl was traveling by ship with her family. The captain's wife told the child that the captain had a bird of paradise. She was captivated by the description of the bird and longed to see it for herself. So the nurse left the child on the deck and went to find the captain. The child could not bear to wait, and asked the steward on board to take her at once to see the bird of paradise. The steward did not know that her legs could not walk, and simply took her along to see that beautiful bird. A miracle happened: because of her overwhelming longing, the child forgot herself, grasped the steward's hand, and slowly began to walk. From then on, the child's illness was cured. When the girl grew up, she threw herself self-forgetfully into literary creation, and in the end became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature; she was Selma Lagerlof.

blocks.text: The Latest Psychological Therapies for Cancer Patients

inline.s: In ancient China, physicians had already noticed the role played by mental factors in the occurrence and development of tumors and other diseases. Once cancer is discovered, the patient's mind suffers a great blow, and emotions such as fear, anger, and despair arise one after another, seriously affecting the effectiveness of treatment throughout the whole course of therapy. In clinical work we see that under the same medical conditions, some patients who are able to "take things in stride" and possess a firm will to struggle against disease often respond to treatment far better than those patients who are frightened out of their wits by cancer. If one's spirit is crushed, then even the best treatment is in vain. Of course, correct and timely diagnosis and treatment, when they achieve results, in turn fill the patient with confidence in recovery and strengthen his fighting spirit. Emotions can both "cause cancer" and "cure cancer." Therefore, in addition to actively pursuing clinical medical treatment, tumor patients should also attend early to their spiritual and psychological recovery.
Now, an introduction to the latest psychological therapies for cancer patients:

1. Faith therapy: Scientific research proves that every person possesses an extraordinary potential. Once it is aroused, it will bring a person unexpected gains, and may even produce miracles. Faith can arouse this potential. Therefore, after falling ill, one should as quickly as possible shake off negative emotions and resolve, no matter how much suffering must be endured, to fight the disease tenaciously. Believe that a miracle will happen in your own case.

2. Imagination therapy: During radiation therapy, one can imagine the rays killing the cancer cells in one's body. When at leisure, the patient imagines his whole body unobstructed and free-flowing, somewhat like yoga. When practicing imagination therapy, the body must be relaxed and distracting thoughts cast aside.

3. Reassurance therapy: It is an excellent remedy for treating cancer. This requires the help of family members, friends, and doctors, helping the patient shed mental burdens and dispel worries. In reassurance therapy one should be sincere and warm, never perfunctory, evasive, or deceitful, though one may dwell on the light and avoid the heavy.

4. Saliva-swallowing therapy: Scientists suggest that when eating one must chew well and swallow slowly. If there is time, one may try saliva-swallowing therapy: the patient calms his mind, gently breathes out three times, then extends the tongue outside the teeth but inside the lips, and stirs it up and down, left and right. When the mouth is full of saliva, rinse and swish it
times, then, with intention, send the saliva slowly down into the dantian in five portions. Repeat each practice three times,
times daily. Persevere, and there may be unexpected results.
5. Music therapy: that is, listening to music, but the listening time should not be too long, and the volume is best kept below
decibels.
6. Humor therapy: Medical scientists have found that cancer patients who laugh regularly can have their condition eased.

blocks.text: Psychological Suggestion Therapy for Cancer Patients

inline.s: Suggestion therapy is an ancient yet genuinely effective and commonly used method of psychological treatment. It is called ancient because in certain primitive superstitious healing activities such as divination and praying to spirits, suggestion was plainly present. Since the profession of doctor came into being, physicians - especially those of greater renown - have consciously or unconsciously employed suggestion therapy in the course of practice, and suggestion therapy is indeed effective. There was once a report saying: there was a woman patient over
years of age who complained of muscle spasms in both legs and of weakness and lack of strength; a
CT
scan confirmed that she had a huge tumor (

cm), and surgery was prepared at once. But because the patient feared surgery, she sought treatment from a Chinese medicine doctor and took Chinese herbs for more than a year; she felt the weakness in her legs growing worse, often sensed that death was near, and lived in constant terror. Clinging to a slender hope of survival, the patient found a psychotherapist. On careful inquiry it was learned that

years earlier it had begun when her husband died suddenly of illness and she grieved excessively. So he decided to use suggestion therapy. He said to the patient: "What you have is not a brain tumor; you will certainly not die, and you need not take any more medicine. As long as every day you think more about and do more of the things that make you happy, and listen to cheerful music, your legs will be able to walk and your illness will be cured." When the patient heard this she was at first delighted, and soon afterward half-believing, but she did as she was told, and indeed within a few days the symptom of leg weakness improved markedly. Afterward he encouraged and guided her many times more, strengthening her confidence.

years have passed, and she is still living very well. Of course this is a rather special case, but the example of a doctor's words, expressions, and other suggestions markedly improving a patient's general symptoms is something almost every medical worker has experienced.

Suggestion therapy can be carried out directly, as in the example above, which is direct suggestion; it can also be combined with other treatments - for instance, various drugs, physical therapy, qigong, and so on paired with suggestion therapy often produce unexpected results. Suggestion therapy can further be divided into "hetero-suggestion," that is, suggestion conveyed through others, and "auto-suggestion," that is, the patient suggesting a certain idea to himself. Some clinical medical experts have found that through imagination (auto-suggestion) the number of immune cells can be increased, with varying efficacy for all kinds of patients (from cancer down to the common cold). For example, in the United States there was a woman patient with a malignant tumor on her neck; the doctors concluded that she had only

months to live. Later, on the advice of a medical psychology expert, she adopted "imagination therapy." Every day she sat quietly on her bed, free of distracting thoughts, concentrating on imagining that the tumor on her neck was a demon, while the white blood cells in her body were brave knights brandishing sharp swords to attack the demon and gradually wiping the demon out completely. Each day she imagined this
times. A year later, the patient did not die on schedule, but miraculously recovered. According to American experts' statistics,
cancer patients declared by hospitals to have less than a year to live, after treatment with imagination therapy, lived at least
months, and

of the patients partly or fully recovered their health. The principle of imagination therapy may be that it makes use of some connection existing between the brain and the body's immune system; imagination improves the body's immune function, thereby effectively restraining the progress of disease. At present imagination therapy has abroad become a necessary prescription for treating "terminal illnesses"; this prescription can at least strengthen patients' confidence in overcoming disease and lighten their mental pressure, and is undoubtedly beneficial to recovery.

When using suggestion therapy, there must certainly be guidance from a medical psychology expert, and it must never be used indiscriminately. Moreover, although a doctor's words and expressions can serve as means of suggestion to treat illness, harmful suggestion can produce serious consequences. In addition, suggestion therapy can produce different effects in different people.
Suggestion therapy (S
uggestive therapy

) refers to a method of psychological treatment that uses verbal or nonverbal means to guide the patient to comply docilely and passively with the doctor's opinions, thereby achieving a certain therapeutic purpose.

Suggestion therapy is very closely related to hypnosis; in a sense, hypnosis is a form of suggestion - that is, suggestion given to the patient not in a waking state but in a hypnotic state. So-called suggestion refers to the psychological phenomenon in which a person or an environment sends certain information to an individual in an unobtrusive way, and the individual is unwittingly influenced by this information and acts accordingly. It is a supposition affirmed by subjective will; it need not be grounded in fact, but because the subject has affirmed its existence, the mind strives toward this content with all its might.

The history of suggestion therapy is ancient and long. Mesmer's hypnotic performances aroused people's inquiry into its mysteries. Charcot, Pavlov, Freud, and others all offered many incisive discussions of the phenomenon of suggestion. Pavlov said: "Suggestion is the simplest and most typical conditioned reflex of man." The famous American psychologist
William
James (in English, W
illiam James
), in the

s of this century wrote the book The Psychology of Suggestion, while the famous British psychologist McDougall's clinical application of it was unsurpassed and won him a resounding reputation. During the First World War, a psychological phobia - "shell shock" - prevailed on the British front lines, brought on by the shock of bomb explosions; in severe cases the limbs were paralyzed. There was no cure for this illness, and it spread rather quickly, giving the British authorities a headache. At this point McDougall joined the wartime treatment; after investigation he found that it was a "mind illness," and so, relying on his former social prestige, he successfully carried out suggestive psychotherapy. With a pen he drew a circle on the soldier's leg a few inches below the knee, where the lower limb had lost sensation, then told the patient in an unquestionable tone that tomorrow the part below the circle would certainly return to normal. The next day, the soldier indeed regained sensation. Day after day he raised the position of the circle in this way, until the soldier was fully cured.
. Suggestive psychotherapy carried out in the waking state can be divided into two major categories: hetero-suggestion therapy and auto-suggestion therapy.

) Hetero-suggestion is suggestion imposed on the patient by the therapist. It works mainly through the doctor's prestige in the patient's eyes to suggest a certain idea to the patient, thereby enhancing and improving his mental state, regulating his behavior and the physiological functions of his body, and achieving the goal of curing disease. Hetero-suggestion therapy is quite widely used in clinical practice. Once, a patient came to a hospital, saying how very uncomfortable he was. The doctor gave him a thorough physical examination and found every part of his body perfectly healthy, with nothing wrong at all; yet the patient was indeed wasting away day by day, and there was nothing to be done. Later a psychotherapist took on this patient and conducted a most solemn and thorough examination, then said to him: I have finally discovered it - what you have is a syndrome. He also told him that a specific remedy had just been successfully tested, made especially for this illness, and that one injection would guarantee recovery in three days. Three days after the injection, the patient was indeed lively and well again. In fact, what the psychotherapist injected was only glucose solution; what truly cured the illness was the suggestive power of words. Besides this, in hetero-suggestion therapy there are also nonverbal suggestion methods, such as the doctor, or the doctor mobilizing the patient's family or fellow patients, using posture, facial expression, and the environment to exert a certain influence.

) Auto-suggestion therapy is a method of psychological treatment in which the patient, through his own cognition, speech, thinking, and other mental processes, regulates and changes his physical and mental state. The power of auto-suggestion is truly astonishing. Under the influence of auto-suggestion, a person can suddenly become deaf or impaired, simply because the functions of the corresponding areas of the brain governing vision and hearing have been disturbed, forming a pathological inhibitory center that makes the nerve cells lose their normal working function. They no longer receive incoming information, and of course cannot respond to it. Such a patient can be treated with hypnotic suggestion therapy, and can be cured at once, astonishing those who do not know the truth.

A man walked into a cold-storage room and was inadvertently locked inside. At first he did not mind and did not feel cold; later, when he looked up and saw the word "Freezing," he was instantly seized with tension. A threat of death enveloped his heart. The more he thought, the more frightened he became; the more he thought, the colder he felt; in the end he curled up into a ball and died in terror. In fact, the refrigeration unit in the room had not been turned on, and the cold was far from enough to kill a person. It was entirely due to the power of auto-suggestion that he died: fear caused a sharp secretion of adrenaline, cardiovascular disturbance, and necrosis of heart function.

Because the effects of auto-suggestion are enormous, an American medical professor proposed a new theory about the cause of cancer, holding that the development of cancer is mainly not a matter of cancer cells objectively present, but rather that subjective emotions and auto-suggestion bring about cancerous change. Although this theory has not been widely accepted, it is undeniable that once cancer patients learn the truth about their illness, their condition changes drastically. Therefore, in the course of psychological treatment, on the one hand the therapist's diagnostic and therapeutic language and behavior are extremely important and should be used with care, lest negative suggestion occur; on the other hand, the therapist must inspire and guide the patient to exercise the regulating power of self-awareness, to eliminate those auto-suggestions that add to his mental burden and harm his mental health, and to cultivate positive, optimistic auto-suggestions, so that they develop in a direction conforming to the requirements of treatment and conducive to dispelling the symptoms.

. There are two ways of applying suggestion therapy: direct and indirect. Direct suggestion therapy means having the patient sit quietly in a comfortable, quiet chair while the therapist, with skillful language or expression, gives guidance and suggestion to the patient, so that the patient accepts the suggestion and thereby changes his original pathological sensations and unhealthy attitudes, achieving the therapeutic goal. Indirect suggestion therapy is suggestion treatment carried out with the aid of some stimulus or the cooperation of an instrument examination and reinforced by language. Clinically, one may use physical examination procedures on the patient, or use a certain instrument, or inject certain drugs, or place the patient in certain specific environments, and then combine these with the therapist's verbal attitude to give suggestion, thereby making the suggestive effect more pronounced. For example, in treating hysterical limb paralysis, the therapist may use electrical stimulation of the muscles while, in an even and forceful tone, using prepared suggestive phrases such as, "Your limb has been electrified, the nerve currents are gradually flowing freely, and the muscles are beginning to gain strength," to give the patient positive suggestion, thereby achieving a good therapeutic result.
. Suggestion therapy is usually combined with certain auxiliary means to improve efficacy. Commonly used methods include: giving the patient some side-effect-free "placebo,"
ml of

% calcium gluconate injected intravenously, or distilled water injected intradermally; electroacupuncture physiotherapy, and so on. In clinical application, suggestion therapy is mainly used to treat neurosis, hysterical paraplegia, hysterical amaurosis, hysterical mutism, hysterical asthma, obsessive-compulsive disorder, stuttering, motor disorders, and certain psychosomatic diseases.

Suggestion therapy is one method of psychological treatment, and for various forms of hysterical attack it can sometimes produce immediate results. So-called suggestion means that when a person is in a certain specific environment and emotional context, he often unconditionally accepts external influences or ideas. Hysterical patients are often readily susceptible to suggestion; they may fall ill because of suggestion, and often may also be cured by accepting suggestion. Physicians of successive dynasties in our country also attached great importance to this and were skilled in applying suggestion therapy. For example, the Jingyue Quanshu records that the famous Ming dynasty physician Zhang Jingyue one day went to see a prostitute suffering an acute attack. Zhang saw that she was foaming at the mouth, lying stiffly on the ground, her mouth and nose cold, her breath seemingly gone; he felt her pulse and found it gentle and regular as usual - the pulse signs and the symptoms were utterly inconsistent - and judged it to be hysteria. Zhang said loudly: "This person's illness is very dangerous and requires fire treatment, using large moxa cones to cauterize the brow, the philtrum, and the lower abdomen, otherwise her life will be hard to save. I have moxa wool at my lodging; fetch it quickly for use." Then he stopped and said: "Wait - I have medicine with me. If she can swallow it, and there is sound and breath after swallowing, then there is no need for moxa; if she cannot swallow, or if there is no sound after swallowing, then moxibustion will not be too late." When the prostitute heard Zhang Jingyue's words, the medicine had barely reached her lips when she immediately swallowed it; thereupon sound came forth, her body moved, and her illness was cured.

Normal people can all accept suggestion, but not everyone is highly suggestible; the capacity to accept suggestion varies from person to person. Only in those who are readily suggestible can the application of suggestion therapy produce a therapeutic effect. Before carrying out suggestion treatment, one must explain matters to the patient's relatives or colleagues and gain their cooperation; otherwise, their inappropriate suggestions may cause the treatment to fail. There are many methods of suggestion treatment, and different therapeutic methods may be adopted for different forms of attack. Generally, language combined with drugs or physical therapy is most often used. For hysterical convulsions, strong acupuncture stimulation is often used; for hysterical blindness and loss of voice, intravenous injection of calcium gluconate may be used. All the treatments described above work under verbal suggestion.

Hypnotherapy is a kind of suggestion therapy, and generally has fairly good efficacy for more intractable hysterical attacks or for patients for whom other therapies have failed. This method puts the patient into a hypnotic state so that the influence of language is reinforced and the suggestive effect strengthened. At present, clinically, drug-induced hypnosis is mostly used: during treatment the patient lies in a quiet environment with limbs relaxed, then is given a slow intravenous injection of

amobarbital sodium or thiopental sodium; while injecting, one talks with the patient, or has the patient count numbers, and when the patient's speech becomes slow and indistinct, it means he has entered the hypnotic state. At this point the doctor may carry out treatment according to the planned regimen - for example, inducing recollection of past events, which the patient can recall one by one; or having him move the paralyzed limb or vocalize, all of which can be done. After the patient enters the hypnotic state, the speed of injection must be slowed to prevent him from falling asleep. When terminating treatment, one may continue to push the drug so that he enters sleep; after resting a while, when he wakes, everything can return to normal.

blocks.text: Why Suggestion Therapy Can Cure Disease

inline.s: Any therapy for treating disease, besides having its theoretical basis, must also have its practical basis. The fundamental reason why suggestion therapy, with its long history, can cure disease is at present generally considered to be the result of suggestion and of its effects.

First, suggestion can exert a marked influence on an individual's physiological activity. A great many facts show that after a person accepts suggestion, he can not only change the state of activity of the voluntary muscles but also affect the function of the involuntary muscles, and may even experience various hallucinations; some cases verge on the "miraculous" and are hard to fathom. Someone once performed an experiment like this: a fulcrum was placed at the center of a wooden board, and the subject was made to lie on the board and keep the original state of balance; then he was told to imagine in his mind the scene of riding a bicycle and pedaling with his feet, but without making any actual movement. After a period of such suggestion, there generally appeared the phenomenon that the end near the feet sank and the end near the head rose, destroying the original balance. Research confirmed that this was because, under the influence of the idea of pedaling hard himself, the subject's lower limbs produced an ideational movement, and this ideational movement caused dilation of the blood vessels of the lower limbs, increased blood flow, and relatively increased weight, thereby destroying the balance.

In addition, suggestion also has a marked effect on the body’s organs and sensations. There was once a well-known cardiovascular physician who, after carefully studying his own heart’s function, was able to feel the contraction and dilation of his own heart; thereupon a racing heartbeat and an irregular rhythm appeared, and only after going away to rest for a time did he recover.

Other experiments likewise fully demonstrate the effect of suggestion. If one gives a person the suggestion of being full, it results in an increase of white blood cells in the blood, a phenomenon that appears only after genuine eating; and when one gives a person the suggestion of hunger, there appears the same lowering of the white blood cell count in the blood as in genuine hunger. When suggestion produces a sensation of cold, the oxygen drawn in and the carbon dioxide breathed out increase by

percent, which is identical to breathing in a state of genuine cold. There is likewise a “false burn” occurring in individuals highly susceptible to suggestion: when a wooden stick lightly touches the subject’s skin and it is suggested that a red-hot iron is branding him, after a while the touched area will convincingly turn red or raise blisters.

Whether it is self-suggestion or suggestion from another, it has a clear effect on a person’s psychology and behavior. The familiar tale of “gazing at plums to quench one’s thirst” is the result of the effect of suggestion. Again, when a person rises in the morning, looks in the mirror, finds his face unsightly, dark rings around his eyes, and puffy eyelids, he at once feels limp all over, aches in his back and legs, and resolves to go to the hospital for a checkup instead of to work—this is due to self-suggestion. Moreover, the “false pregnancy” seen in some women is also connected to a mental state that eagerly desires pregnancy; under the influence of this suggestion, when the period is delayed a few days she believes she has conceived and shows certain reactions of pregnancy. This too is the result of self-suggestion.

Furthermore, it should be noted that the effect of suggestion upon an individual under hypnosis is even more pronounced than in the waking state. Under hypnosis the individual enters a special state in which the threshold of consciousness is extremely narrow, giving rise to quite extraordinary physiological reactions. For example, give a hypnotized subject a cup of plain water and suggest that it is sugar water, and upon a blood test one will find that the sugar content of the blood has markedly increased. Through hypnotic suggestion, the hypnotized person may also display a “false death”: “the breathing stops and the heartbeat ceases.” The influence of hypnosis upon a person’s behavior and motives is chiefly seen in the hypnotized person’s absolute obedience to the words of the operator. Not only does he carry out the instructions completely during the hypnosis, but after waking he likewise does so as a matter of course. Hypnosis can even create hallucinations or summon up memories of things that had vanished from consciousness.

From the various effects of suggestion described above we can see that negative suggestion can cause a person to fall ill, while under the influence of positive suggestion an individual can improve and enhance his psychology, his behavior, and the physiological functions of his body—so that suggestion becomes a method for treating illness.
